A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same POSSM study. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete supplements are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching retained content across appendix renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original reaching, handwriting, and speech decoding experiments, computational benchmarks, and supplementary analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds mouse running-speed decoding, multimodal speech results, and architectural and finetuning comparisons.

M1.justification: The central POSSM architecture and UI/full-finetuning procedures remain intact. v2 adds exploratory adaptations: multimodal speech inputs, feature mixers, a recurrent encoder, and LoRA embedding finetuning (Sections 3.3 and D.7–D.9). Its newly documented delimiter omission and clarified speech convolution do not establish changes to the original implementation.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained primate reaching and human tasks, v2 evaluates mouse running-speed decoding from visual and subcortical regions using the Allen Visual Behaviour Neuropixels dataset (D.4). It also adds speech inputs combining spike counts with spiking-band powers and forecasting targets 50 or 100 ms beyond each input chunk, substantially broadening the tested populations, inputs, and task requirements.

E2.justification: The original task-level baseline sets are retained. New appendix comparisons evaluate LoRA against UI (Table 12) and a GRU encoder against standard cross-attention (Table 11), providing a limited expansion of evaluated alternatives.

E3.justification: Reported NHP pretraining expands from 140 to 148 sessions, including 2 to 10 Churchland sessions. POYO's stated learning rate changes from 1.5625e-4 to 0.004 for single-session and 0.002 for pretrained models (S.3.1 versus C.1). Added experiments introduce forecasting horizons, bin-level timestamp controls, and chunk-reset recurrent encoders. These are documented setting changes; they do not establish that every retained experiment was rerun. Table 4 also changes its counting scope to include training, validation, and testing subsets.

E4.justification: v2 retains the existing chunk-size, handwriting-context, and bidirectional-speech analyses. Sections D.5–D.9 add substantial tests of forecasting flexibility, precise spike timing, feature mixers, recurrent versus attention encoders, and LoRA versus UI, directly examining architectural choices and adaptation efficiency.

E5.justification: Table 2 adds paired t-tests against POSSM-GRU and clarifies aggregation over nine sessions and three seeds; three-seed handwriting training was already documented in v1. Speech results are newly described as averages over three seeds, with all standard deviations below 0.1% (Tables 3 and 7; C.3). This establishes expanded reporting, not an explicit increase in runs.

E6.justification: Table 1 revises pretrained-model scores, and Table 2 changes finetuned handwriting results, switching the best backbone from S4D to Mamba. Changed pretraining prevents interpreting these as controlled same-setting gains. Table 3 adds multimodal PERs of 19.80% for POSSM-GRU and 21.74% for GRU. New mouse results and Tables 8–12 expand the findings substantially. Figure 4's few-shot curves change, and Table 6 revises o-POSSM-Mamba UI on C–CO 2010 from 0.6888 to 0.7175.

T1.justification: Section 2.2 corrects incompatible token-matrix dimensions and projection order. Appendix B.2 revises the GRU candidate-state equation and explicitly introduces continuous-to-discrete S4 parameter conversion before constructing the convolution kernel, which v1 omitted. These are limited mathematical corrections and clarifications; no new theorem or proof appears.

C1.justification: The abstract and four introductory contributions remain substantively unchanged. Section 5 modestly strengthens the performance assertion from 'approaching' to 'achieving' state-of-the-art performance for several decoding tasks, while retaining the same efficiency, generalization, and cross-species-transfer contributions.

C2.justification: v2 interprets the new controls as evidence for precise spike timing and cross-attention, identifies a performance-versus-size/latency tradeoff for feature mixers, and presents LoRA as an efficient UI alternative. Section 3.3 adds an interpretation concerning input-modality flexibility. The principal offline-evaluation qualification and clinical-deployment cautions remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds optimizer identities, delimiter-token omission, normalization/feed-forward details, fivefold centre-out loss weighting, and exclusion of perturbed Area2 trials. Reported pretraining resources change from two A100 GPUs for two days to four H100 GPUs for about 36 hours. It adds a project-page link and prospective torch_brain release information, without establishing actual availability. Conversely, the shortened Perich reference loses its explicit versioned dataset identifier.

R1.justification: v2 adds focused references on real-time neuroscience, LFADS, state-space and multimodal methods, optimizers, Allen data, and LoRA. It corrects BRAND's description from non-invasive to invasive recordings and removes the separate Perceiver citation while retaining Perceiver IO. The overarching research positioning remains; publication and bibliography updates are not new contributions.

P1.justification: The main narrative and section order remain stable, with local editing and clearer architecture, speech, and training explanations. Supplementary sections S.1–S.4 become A–D, with additional subsections and a NeurIPS checklist. These extend the existing organization without extensively rewriting the central argument.

P2.justification: The supplement gains a substantial series of comparison displays, Tables 8–12. Table 3 adds a multimodal block, and Table 2 adds significance annotations and an expanded caption. Figure 6 is redesigned from vertically stacked to side-by-side panels; existing tables are restyled and the document reflows. Most original diagrams remain intact.

improvement.justification: v1 demonstrates strong benchmark performance but lacks direct controls isolating precise spike timing and encoder choice. v2's controlled comparisons in Tables 9–11 substantially strengthen the empirical justification for the central architecture. Statistical tests for handwriting transfer and clearer implementation details further improve evidential support and reproducibility. Several extensions remain preliminary, evaluation remains offline, and code access is prospective, but the added validation addresses an important weakness in v1.
